newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end higher; unfazed by Fed meeting. [CORRECTED 22:13 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Stocks end higher; unfazed by Fed meeting. [CORRECTED 22:13 GMT]

text.p: Stocks closed on an upbeat note Monday as Wall Street was unfazed by the possibility the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates at its policy-setting meeting on Tuesday.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 34.21 points to 7,228.88, bouncing back from Friday's sell-off of nearly 140 points. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,390 to 1,056 on light volume of 345 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

With Wall Street investors reluctant to make big trades prior to Tuesday's meeting of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, activity was lighter than usual, which may have exaggerated the market's swings.

Economists are split nearly down the middle about the outcome of the Fed's deliberations, with a slight majority forecasting no change in monetary policy, according to a Reuters survey released Monday.

The inflation-fighting Fed raised short term interest rates by a quarter point at its last meeting in March but the gauges of inflation since then have shown some softening in the economy and few signs of price pressure.
Some analysts said the Fed's stated goal, that it could take 'pre-emptive' steps to fight against future inflation, would likely bring a raise in interest rates.
"It's a close call, but the Fed will probably tighten 25 basis points (one quarter percentage point)," said Frank McCormick, vice president and senior economist at Bank of America.
"The trend rate of GDP growth is about 4 percent, unemployment is down to 4.9 percent and there are some slight signs that core inflation is beginning to pick up," he said.
Traders were also optimistic that a modest rise in rates would not crimp stock prices.

Frank Calta, a trader at Dain Bosworth, said, "If the FOMC raises rates by 25 basis points, it's already in the market and not a big deal. If they raise rates 50 basis points, that's negative for the market. If they don't raise rates, it's a positive but not a blowout positive."

Business was slow in bonds, with the 30-year Treasury bond off 5/32, which raised (corrects from "lowered") its yield to 6.92 (corrects from "6.90") percent from 6.91 percent at Friday's close. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The Dow index was boosted by gains in drug stocks, tobacco, and a jump in Walt Disney Co.

Disney's ABC Network said it would bring back the "Wonderful World of Disney" on Sunday nights and air a second hour of the popular news programme "20/20" on Thursdays. Disney closed up 2-1/8 to 83-1/4.
Tobacco stocks rallied on speculation that a settlement to resolve litigation against the industry could be reached within two to three weeks.
Philip Morris, the most heavily-traded issue on the NYSE, rose 5/8 to 43. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. added 3/8 to 31-3/8.
American Express jumped 1-1/4 to 68-5/8. It signed 21-year-old golf sensation Tiger Woods as a worldwide spokesman.
The strength in blue chip stocks masked some pockets of weakness in the broader market.

On the Nasdaq market, PairGain Technologies Inc. lost more ground, falling 1-3/4 to 15-1/2 on concerns about pricing pressure in its core business and fears that the company might not keep pace with new technology developments.
Concerns about growth hit several technology sectors. Disk drive maker Seagate Technology Inc. lost 3-1/2 at 45.
The Nasdaq Composite index edged up 0.51 of a point to 1,341.24.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 3.52 points to 833.27. The American Stock Exchange index was up 0.76 to 587.48.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.70 to 434.14. The average share was up 16 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,861.067 up 28.662 or 0.37 percent.
